Source. The harness admits only the exact 512-byte witness, so this first project-side use of attacker-controlled input materializes `out_size = 768` as the initial JSON buffer budget for the vulnerable conversion path.

The derived budget is allocated as one SDS string. `flb_sds_create_size(768)` yields `alloc = 768` plus one terminator byte; together with the SDS header this is the 785-byte heap region named by ASan, and all later serializer writes target this same `out_buf`.

The same raw buffer is parsed into the first MessagePack object that `msgpack2json()` will walk. A static replay of the saved bytes shows this call consumes the first 388 bytes as a 15-entry map, and that its top-level map key at index 9 has raw bytes `e0e0e000012a0200a50200a5888888f288888800`.

The serializer enters `msgpack2json()` with logical payload limit `left = json_size - 1 = 767` on the SDS from step 2. The saved stack frame at `msgpack2json:616` shows the later crash occurs while this root map is being walked under that shared `off` and `left` budget.

At frame `msgpack2json:528`, the exact crashing `MSGPACK_OBJECT_STR` is the top-level root-map key at index 9 (10th pair) with bytes `e0e0e000012a0200a50200a5888888f288888800`. `msgpack2json()` has just emitted that key's opening quote at output offset 723, so `flb_utils_write_str()` receives this key with `*off = 724`, `size = left = 767`, and `available = 43`.

The guard immediately above only checked `(available - written) < 6`, which passes because step 6 left exactly 6 bytes, but this `snprintf` returns `len = 7` for `\\u88208`.
The unchecked Unicode escape from step 7 copies 7 bytes at output offsets 761 through 767 and leaves `p = 768`, one byte farther than the six-byte check budget allowed.

After step 8, `written` becomes 44 while the call's `available` from step 5 remained 43. The next guard reuses `available - written` as a `size_t`, so the subtraction wraps instead of going negative and no longer blocks later escapes in this same `flb_utils_write_str()` invocation.
